## Abstract

We classify the weak*-closed maximal left ideals of the measure algebra M(G) for certain Hermitian locally compact groups G in terms of the irreducible representations of G and their asymptotic properties. In particular, we obtain a classification for connected nilpotent Lie groups, and the Euclidean rigid motion groups. We also prove a version of this result for certain weighted measure algebras. We apply our classification to obtain an analogue of Barnes' Theorem on integrable representations for representations vanishing at infinity. We next study the relationship between weak*-closedness and finite generation, proving that in many cases M(G) has no finitely-generated maximal left ideals. We also show that the measure algebra of the 2D Euclidean rigid motion group has a weak*-closed maximal left ideal that is not generated by a projection, and investigate whether or not it has any weak*-closed left ideals which are not finitely-generated.

8. Open Questions

We conclude this article with some problems for future study. The main question we would like

to resolve is whether or not Conjecture 1.1 and Conjecture 1.2 hold for all Hermitian locally

compact groups. Another of the central topics of this article is the connection between ﬁnite

generation of a closed left ideal of a measure algebra, and weak*-closedness. This suggests to

us the following natural questions that we have been unable to answer.

Question 8.1. (i) Does there exist a locally compact group G, and a closed left ideal J

in M p G q, such that J is weak*-closed, but not ﬁnitely-generated?

(ii) Does there exist a locally compact group G, and a closed left ideal J in M p G q, such

that J is ﬁnitely-generated but not generated by a projection?

It would be particularly interesting to be able to answer these questions for maximal left

ideals.

In [19] it was shown that, if G is a non-discrete locally compact group, then L 1 p G q has no

ﬁnitely-generated maximal modular left ideals. It would be interesting to know whether the

same holds for an inﬁnite discrete group G. We saw in Theorem 1.3 that this does hold when

G is ﬁnitely-generated and virtually nilpotent.

Blow-up analysis and compactness for critical Dirac equations on $\mathbb S^n$

Ting Li, Zhongwei Tang

arXiv:2610.33507

Authors: Ting Li, Zhongwei Tang

Submitted: Oct 2026 | Updated: Oct 2026

We study blow-up and compactness for the critical nonlinear Dirac equation \[ D_{g_0}ψ_i = H_i|ψ_i|^{\frac{2}{n-1}}ψ_i \qquad \text{on }\mathbb S^n,\quad n\ge 3, \] where $g_0$ is the round metric and $H_i\to H>0$ in $C^0(\mathbb S^n)$. Under a first-threshold bound on the critical mass, we prove that every blowing-up sequence has, after passing to a subsequence, a unique blow-up point $p$ satisfying $H(p)=\max_{\mathbb S^n}H$. The rescaled solutions converge to a ground-state Dirac bubble that carries the entire limiting critical mass. Under local uniform $C^1$ bounds on $H_i$, we use the Kelvin transform and a second rescaling to prove that $p$ is an isolated simple blow-up point. We also derive sharp pointwise and gradient estimates in cylindrical coordinates and identify the normalized Green limit. If the coefficients converge in $C^2$ near $p$, the Pohozaev identity yields $\operatorname{Hess}_{g_0}H(p)=0$. Consequently, if a positive $H\in C^2(\mathbb S^n)$ satisfies $Δ_{g_0}H(p)<0$ at every global maximum, then solutions with critical mass bounded by a level slightly above the first threshold are uniformly bounded in $L^\infty(\mathbb S^n)$. This bound remains uniform under small $C^2$ perturbations of $H$.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Exact statement

Prove that there exists an absolute epsilon > 0 such that every monic integer polynomial P with Mahler measure M(P) > 1 satisfies M(P) >= 1 + epsilon, or construct a sequence of such polynomials whose Mahler measures decrease to 1.

### Why it matters

A gap would give a uniform restriction on how close these algebraic size measurements can come to their minimum above one. A sequence tending to one would show that no universal positive separation exists.
